candidate.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: recognize common adverse effects, provide medication teaching, and distinguish expected effects from symptoms requiring further evaluation.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — niacin flushing management
candidate.educational_objective: Teach evidence-based strategies for niacin extended-release flushing: clinician-approved aspirin shortly before the dose, avoidance of common flushing triggers, appropriate titration, and continued attention to symptoms that could represent a cardiovascular emergency.

options.A: Ask the prescriber whether aspirin is appropriate; when approved, aspirin taken about 30 minutes before niacin can reduce flushing, and alcohol, hot beverages, and spicy foods should be avoided around dosing time.
options.B: Take niacin on a completely empty stomach and rapidly double the dose so tolerance develops faster.
options.C: Use any NSAID automatically before every dose because all NSAIDs are interchangeable with the labeled aspirin strategy.
options.D: Stop all cardiovascular evaluation during flushing because warmth and redness after niacin cannot overlap with symptoms that require urgent assessment.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. Current FDA labeling for niacin extended-release tablets states that flushing is common and may be minimized by aspirin, up to the recommended dose of 325 mg, taken about 30 minutes before niacin when appropriate. The label also advises avoiding alcohol, hot beverages, and spicy foods around the time of dosing. B is incorrect because the dose should be titrated rather than rapidly doubled, and the label advises administration with a low-fat snack rather than on an empty stomach. C overgeneralizes the evidence to all NSAIDs; the current patient instructions specifically describe aspirin. D is unsafe because clients with cardiovascular disease must still distinguish flushing from symptoms of myocardial infarction or other urgent conditions.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Niacin extended-release flushing can often be reduced with clinician-approved aspirin about 30 minutes before dosing and by avoiding alcohol, hot beverages, and spicy foods around the dose; rapid unsupervised dose escalation and blanket substitution of other NSAIDs are not supported by the label.
candidate.source_document_title: Niacin Extended-Release Tablets Prescribing Information and Patient Information
candidate.source_locator: Patient Counseling/Flushing: flushing is common and more likely with initiation or dose increases. Use of Aspirin Medication: aspirin up to the recommended dose of 325 mg approximately 30 minutes before dosing can minimize flushing. Diet: avoid alcohol, hot beverages, and spicy foods around dosing; take extended-release niacin with a low-fat snack. Patient information distinguishes flushing from possible myocardial-infarction symptoms.
